_comment: Guided tour for the flow-map tool in the emtk window. Steps point at real controls and wait for the user to use them -- there is deliberately no 'do it for me' button, because someone who watched a button being pressed has not learned where it is. Targets are the spec's attr names and the buttons and windows the window draws.

steps.title: What this tool measures
steps.text: A flow map is one velocity vector per place in the image: where the sample is moving, and how fast. Nothing is fitted: the velocity is read off where a correlation peak is, not off a parameter released in a transport model. You press the buttons; the tour only points at them.

steps.title: Start with data you can check
steps.text: The hard part of a flow map is knowing whether to believe it: arrows appear over a picture and there is nothing to compare them with. So start with a simulated scan whose flow is known: laminar flow through a channel, fastest in the middle, zero at the walls. It is a real photon stream, written as an ordinary PTU.

await.hint: Press Load demo. The first time it simulates the scan, which takes about twenty seconds; the status line counts the frames.

steps.title: The file is now selected
steps.text: The demo has been written and loaded, and its scanner settings came with it. Any TIFF stack or photon stream can go here instead; it just needs at least three frames, since a flow map measures what moved between them.

steps.title: The scanner clock is the measurement
steps.text: A velocity is a distance over a time, and both come from here, not from the image. The frame time is the clock a STICS velocity is measured against, the pixel size converts pixels into um. An error in either scales every arrow by the same factor with nothing looking wrong. For a real file take them from the acquisition software.

steps.title: Tile size: the resolution of the map
steps.text: Each arrow is computed from one square sub-region. A small tile localizes the flow but holds few molecules and leaves the peak little room to travel; a large tile averages distinct flows into one arrow. Several focus waists across is the usual compromise.

steps.title: Lags: the trap worth knowing
steps.text: The peak travels further the more frames you look ahead, and it must stay inside its tile. A correlation map is periodic, so a peak driven past the edge wraps round to the other side, where a straight line fits a confident velocity pointing the wrong way. Such tiles are refused and counted; if tiles were refused, use fewer lags or a bigger tile.

steps.title: Now measure
steps.text: Every tile gets its own correlation carpet, its peak is tracked across the lag range, and a straight line through those peaks is the velocity.

await.hint: Press Map flow and wait for the status line.

steps.title: Read the arrows
steps.text: Direction first: that is the part a correlation measurement gets right even where the magnitude is conservative. The demo flows along +x, fastest in the middle of the frame. Arrow colour runs from cool for the slowest tile to warm for the fastest, and the caption says how many arrows survived the quality threshold.

steps.title: Check it against the truth
steps.text: The profile collapses the field to one curve across the frame, with the simulated truth drawn beside it. The shape should match: parabolic, peaking in the middle. The recovered magnitude reads low where the flow shears inside a tile: a flow map is a reliable picture of where and a conservative estimate of how fast.

steps.title: Before you believe a real map
steps.text: Four checks: did any tile escape (shorten the lag range)? Does a static region go blank as you raise Min. quality (peak jitter fitted to a line is always some velocity)? Does the other estimator agree? Does reversing the flow reverse the arrows? The Help button has the long version.
